title: Introduction to Data Sufficiency
tagline: Year 2 — Deciding whether the given statements are enough to answer a question

introduction.overview: A data sufficiency question asks a question and gives two statements. You do not have to find the answer; you only decide whether the information in the statements is enough to find a single definite answer. The possible verdicts are: statement I alone is sufficient, statement II alone is sufficient, both together are needed, each alone is sufficient, or even both together are not sufficient.
introduction.placementRelevance: Data sufficiency questions are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds. They test judgment about information rather than calculation, so they are quick when approached systematically.
introduction.realWorldContext: Deciding whether you have enough information to make a decision, such as quoting a project or diagnosing a fault, uses the same judgment.

learningObjectives: Decide whether a statement alone gives a unique answer
Combine statements only when each alone is insufficient
Recognise when the statements are consistent but still not enough
Use the standard order of evaluation
Avoid solving the problem fully when it is not needed

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A unique answer is needed: if a statement gives two possible values (for example, x² = 9), it is insufficient unless extra information fixes the value.

coreDefinitions: Sufficient: the information leads to exactly one definite answer.
Insufficient: the information leaves two or more possible answers (or none).
Together: using both statements at the same time.
Yes/no questions: the data is sufficient if it always gives "yes" or always gives "no"; if it can give both, it is insufficient.
Consistency: the statements never contradict each other in a well-posed question.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The question is not "What is the answer?" but "Can I find the answer from this?" A statement is sufficient if, once you know it, only one answer is possible. If a different situation consistent with the statement gives a different answer, it is not sufficient.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Take each statement in turn. Try to imagine two different situations that both satisfy the statement but give different answers to the question. If you can, it is insufficient. Then combine and repeat.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Standard order
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Test I alone → test II alone → test both together
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Stop when a statement is sufficient.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Unique-answer rule
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: One definite value (or a definite yes/no)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Counting unknowns
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: n unknowns need n independent equations
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: x + y = 10 alone is not enough

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Combining statements
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Use both if each alone fails
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The pair may fix the value.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Other possibilities
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If a missing category could exist, the data is insufficient

mainNarrative: Work in a fixed order. First decide whether statement I alone gives a unique answer. Then decide the same for statement II. Only if neither alone is enough, combine them. This order prevents the common error of using both statements when one suffices.

A unique answer is required. "What is the value of x? I. 2x = 10" has the unique answer 5, so I alone is sufficient. If a statement leaves more than one value, such as x² = 9, it is insufficient alone.

Many questions need two items of information. To find a car's speed you need both the distance and the time. Neither alone is enough, but both together are. Similarly, to find Ravi's age from "he is 5 years older than Sita" you also need Sita's age.

Yes/no questions: "Is the number even? I. It is divisible by 4." Every multiple of 4 is even, so the answer is always yes, which is sufficient. If a statement leaves both yes and no possible, it is insufficient.

Beware of hidden possibilities. "How many marbles are in the bag? I. 12 are red. II. Red marbles are three times the blue ones." Even together, there may be marbles of other colours, so the total cannot be found.

deepDiveAspects.title: Do not solve fully
deepDiveAspects.content: You only need to decide whether the answer can be found. Avoid long calculations when a quick check of "unique or not" is enough.

deepDiveAspects.title: Counter-example method
deepDiveAspects.content: To show insufficiency, give two different cases that both satisfy the statement but give different answers.

problemVariations.exampleSnippet: Area of a square with side 6

solvedExamples.title: Both needed
solvedExamples.question: What is the speed of the car? I. The car travelled 120 km. II. The journey took 2 hours.

steps.title: I alone
steps.explanation: Distance alone does not give speed.

steps.title: II alone
steps.explanation: Time alone does not give speed.

solvedExamples.title: One statement enough
solvedExamples.question: What is the value of x? I. 2x = 10. II. x + y = 8.

steps.title: II alone
steps.explanation: Two unknowns, one equation: not unique.

solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using both when one is enough.

solvedExamples.title: Even both not sufficient
solvedExamples.question: How many marbles are in the bag? I. 12 are red. II. Red marbles are three times the blue ones.

steps.title: Total
steps.explanation: Other colours may exist, so the total is unknown.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Even both together are not sufficient
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The statements do not mention other colours.

shortcutMethods.title: Order and counter-example

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Test I, then II, then both. For each, look for two different cases that fit but give different answers.

rulesForApplication: Yes/no: always yes or always no.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using both when one is enough

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: If the verdict is "I alone", options saying "II alone" can be removed only after checking II.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Follow the I, II, both order.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I test one statement at a time?
